alignment.note: Greek and Latin render the recollection with an aorist/perfect passive participle (ἀναμνησθείς / recordatus); Syriac uses a finite verb ܘܐܬܕܟܪ ('and he remembered'), folding the conjunction into the verbal form rather than a participial circumstantial clause.

Greek names the apostle by his Greek surname ὁ Πέτρος ('the Rock', with the article) and Latin follows as Petrus; the Peshitta retains the original Semitic name ܫܡܥܘܢ (Simon/Shemʿon), reflecting Syriac onomastic preference for the Aramaic form over the Greek translation of the cognomen.
Greek uses the historic present λέγει ('says'), a vivid Markan stylistic feature; both Syriac ܘܐܡܪ and Latin dixit normalise to a past-tense ('and said' / 'said'), smoothing the narrative tense.
αὐτῷ / ܠܗ / ei (Latin adds the colon punctuation token introducing direct speech)

Greek marks the noun with a feminine article ἡ συκῆ and Latin uses the bare noun ficus; the Peshitta adds a demonstrative/resumptive pronoun ܗܝ ('that') after ܬܬܐ, anticipating the following relative clause in typical Syriac syntax.
ἣν κατηράσω / ܕܠܛܬ / cui maledixisti — relative clause 'which you cursed'

Greek ἐξήρανται is a perfect passive ('has been/stands dried up'), emphasising the resultant withered state; Syriac ܝܒܫܬ and Latin aruit are simple perfects/preterites ('it withered'), focusing on the completed action rather than the durative result.
